knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 5.1.4
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly pairs simple loss functions with the Bayesian point estimators they typically justify?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Squared error maps to posterior mean; absolute error to median. Credible interval is a set probability statement, not the same object as a point estimator.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Squared-error: posterior mean; absolute-error: posterior median.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Collapsing point estimator into credible interval or swapping mean and median losses.

choices.label: Squared-error loss typically justifies the posterior mean as the Bayesian point estimator. Absolute-error loss typically justifies the posterior median.
The Bayesian point estimator under any loss function is the same object as a credible interval; both summarise posterior uncertainty identically.
Absolute-error loss justifies the posterior mean; squared-error loss justifies the posterior median.
Loss-based estimators always equal the maximum likelihood estimate regardless of the posterior.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 5.1.4
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Posterior for θ is available. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: Name estimators under losses; refuse interval collapse.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Mean under squared error, median under absolute error. Interval and point estimator answer different questions.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Squared-error: mean; absolute-error: median. Refuse interval collapse.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Equating point estimator with credible interval or swapping loss pairings.

choices.label: Under squared-error loss, use the posterior mean as the Bayesian point estimator; under absolute-error loss, use the posterior median. A point estimator summarises the posterior under a loss; a credible interval is a posterior probability set for θ. Different objects.
The Bayesian point estimator under loss is the same object as a credible interval.
Under squared-error loss, use the posterior median; under absolute-error loss, use the posterior mean.
Both losses justify the posterior mode only; mean and median are frequentist labels.

worked_example.title: Squared-error vs absolute-error Bayes estimates
worked_example.problem_statement: A discrete posterior for a reserve parameter θ (£000) places probabilities 0.20, 0.50, 0.30 on the values 1, 2, 3 respectively. Find the Bayes estimate under squared-error loss and under absolute-error loss.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Recall squared-error → posterior mean; absolute-error → posterior median.

steps.label: Squared-error estimate (posterior mean)
steps.explanation: Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean.

steps.label: Absolute-error estimate (posterior median)
steps.attempt_cue: Find the smallest θ with cumulative posterior probability ≥ 0.5.
steps.explanation: Under absolute-error loss, the Bayes estimator is a posterior median.

steps.label: Contrast the two answers
steps.attempt_cue: Note that 2.1 and 2 need not coincide.
steps.explanation: Different loss functions justify different point summaries of the same posterior.
steps.result: Loss choice changes the Bayes estimate

worked_example.final_answer: Squared-error Bayes estimate = 2.1; absolute-error Bayes estimate = 2 (posterior median).
worked_example.common_pitfall: Always reporting the posterior mean regardless of loss, or taking the posterior mode 2 as if it were required by squared-error loss.
